name: Deep jade
lede: Diamine Green is a dark, muted blue-green from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, grouped by the ISCC-NBS system with ordinary moderate greens rather than anything unusual.

sections.title: A moderate green, precisely placed
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 plate VII gives this swatch at hue 37, tone m, and the 1955 ISCC-NBS system puts it in block 145, described as a moderate green [1]. In Munsell terms it reads 8.4G 4.2/4.1 [1]. The name's first word again points to diamine, the family of azo dyes once used on cotton; nothing in the sources checked here explains why this particular green carried it [1].

The closest color in ColorHub's library is [[patina-green]], and the nearest core app color is [[bottle-green]], about six units off [1].

Its Munsell chroma of about 23 makes it a fairly saturated green for such a dark value, more like a dyed cloth than a faded pigment [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this dark green in 62 of 23,781 paintings, about a quarter of one per cent [2]. The earliest match is a 1480 portrait by Hans Memling, well before any dye named diamine existed, so that is a lookalike hue rather than a pigment record, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. The 1900s again stand out, at over four times the paintings' baseline rate [2]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not evidence of a particular pigment or dye [2]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[2].
